paper_metadata.title: Factors Predictive of Outcome in Childhood Epilepsy

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study provides a clear description of the source population, recruitment period, and inclusion/exclusion criteria. However, it is a retrospective review of a single pediatric neurologist's database (convenience sample), which may introduce referral bias. Furthermore, there was a statistically significant difference in etiology between the included subjects and those lost to follow-up, suggesting the analyzed sample may not perfectly represent the initial cohort.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The subjects were identified from a comprehensive computerized database of a single pediatric neurologist (M.I.S.). ... Patients entered into this database were seen by the neurologist in four different clinics: a hospital-based private neurology office... a hospital-based ambulatory clinic... a hospital-based neonatal neurology clinic... and a suburban private pediatric neurology clinic.
items.reasoning: The authors specify the clinical settings and the nature of the practice (referral-based pediatric neurology).

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Children with new-onset epilepsy aged between 2 and 17 years were identified through a systematic search of the above database.
items.reasoning: While the database search is systematic, the population is limited to a single practitioner's patients, which may not represent the broader community of children with epilepsy (referral bias).

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: initial intake and neurologic assessment between July 1, 1991 and June 30, 2000
items.reasoning: The dates are explicitly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Montreal Children's Hospital, Montreal, QC, Canada. ... seen by the neurologist in four different clinics: a hospital-based private neurology office... hospital-based ambulatory clinic... hospital-based neonatal neurology clinic... and a suburban private pediatric neurology clinic.
items.reasoning: The geographic location and specific clinical settings are well-defined.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: All subjects who met the following inclusion criteria were included in the study: (1) initial intake and neurologic assessment between July 1, 1991 and June 30, 2000; (2) epilepsy onset between 2 and 17 years of age; (3) treatment with an antiepileptic drug; and (4) a minimum follow-up of 24 months.
items.reasoning: The criteria are explicit, including age, timeframe, treatment status, and follow-up duration.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: The medical charts of all such potential subjects were retrieved and systematically reviewed
items.reasoning: As a retrospective chart review, 'participation' refers to the inclusion of all eligible records. While they reviewed all potential subjects, the reliance on a single database means we are unsure if this captures the true eligible population in the region.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The clinical features at intake recorded were gender, age at first afebrile seizure, seizure type, the number of seizures prior to treatment, family history of epilepsy, a history of febrile seizures, perinatal history, comorbid conditions, neurologic examination, and the most abnormal electroencephalogram (EEG)
items.reasoning: Table 2 and 3 provide a comprehensive breakdown of baseline clinical and demographic data.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study excluded 44 children (approx 18% of the eligible cohort) due to follow-up < 24 months. Crucially, Table 1 shows a significant difference in etiology between those included and those lost to follow-up (81.8% cryptogenic in lost vs 32.1% in included), which suggests attrition was not random and could bias the prognostic estimates.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Forty-four children were excluded because their duration of follow-up was less than 2 years.
items.reasoning: Approximately 18% of the eligible cohort (44 out of 240) was lost to follow-up, which is near the 20% threshold often used to indicate risk.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study does not describe attempts to contact those lost to follow-up; they were simply excluded based on the 24-month follow-up criterion.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Of these, one patient with dysgerminoma died... five patients moved, and five patients were from northern Quebec and were not seen regularly in follow-up.
items.reasoning: Reasons are provided for 11 of the 44 excluded patients, but the remaining 33 are not specifically accounted for.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The clinical features of the remaining 33 children lost to follow-up and the 196 who met all inclusion criteria are summarized in Table 1.
items.reasoning: Table 1 provides a direct comparison of age, gender, seizure type, and etiology for the lost subjects.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: However, there was a significant difference (P < .001) in the number of children within the three etiologic groups.
items.reasoning: The authors explicitly state that the etiologic distribution was significantly different between the groups, which is a major prognostic factor.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Prognostic factors (seizure types, comorbidities, EEG) were defined using international standards (ILAE, DSM-IV) and recorded prospectively in a database by a single expert, ensuring consistency in measurement across the cohort.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: The seizure type was classified according to the classification of the International League Against Epilepsy. ... ADHD and learning disability were defined according to their respective Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-IV criteria.
items.reasoning: Standardized clinical definitions were used for all primary prognostic factors.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Information is entered into this database by the neurologist at the time of initial consultation and updated subsequently at follow-up visits
items.reasoning: Measurements were made by a specialist at the time of care, reducing recall bias, and used established diagnostic tools (EEG, neuropsychological evaluation).

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: The presence or absence of a given finding at study intake was modeled as a binary variable.
items.reasoning: Variables like age and seizure counts were handled appropriately, and clinical categories (e.g., MR, delay) used standard clinical thresholds.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All children were evaluated by the same physician (M.I.S.) in a similar fashion.
items.reasoning: Consistency is high as a single neurologist performed the assessments.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: The medical charts of all such potential subjects were retrieved and systematically reviewed by one investigator (M.O.)
items.reasoning: The use of a structured database and chart review resulted in complete data for the analyzed cohort.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no mention of missing data or imputation methods, though the N for all tables matches the total sample size.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Outcomes (remission, intractability) were clearly defined based on seizure frequency and medication status. While the retrospective nature means outcome assessment wasn't 'blinded' to prognostic factors, the criteria used (e.g., 24 months seizure-free) are objective clinical milestones.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Remission was defined as successful cessation of medication. ... Intractability was defined as seizures recurring at least monthly for more than a year associated with failure of at least three antiepileptic drugs
items.reasoning: The study provides specific, measurable definitions for all three primary outcomes.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: The hospital records were reviewed for any subsequent visits to the hospital. It is therefore probable that the vast majority of children with recurrent seizures were recognized
items.reasoning: Outcome was determined by clinical follow-up and chart review. While not blinded, the criteria are standard in epilepsy research.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All children were in the study for a period long enough to meet the criteria for remission. ... The last intake date for the study was June 2000, and the patients' charts were reviewed 33 to 35 months later
items.reasoning: The same review process and clinical criteria were applied to the entire cohort.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study used multivariable Cox and logistic regression to adjust for a wide range of potential confounders, including age, etiology, and comorbidities. They also appropriately included duration of follow-up as a covariate in the logistic models to account for the time-dependent nature of epilepsy remission.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: The variables entered into the Cox regression and logistic regression models were gender; age at onset of seizures; abnormal perinatal history; family history of epilepsy; developmental delay at onset; mental retardation at onset; learning disability at onset; ADHD at onset; pyramidal tract signs at initial examination; number of seizures prior to treatment; EEG abnormality; cryptogenic epilepsy; remote symptomatic epilepsy...
items.reasoning: A comprehensive list of clinical and demographic confounders was included.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Global developmental delay was defined as a significant delay in two or more of the following developmental domains... ADHD and learning disability were defined according to their respective Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-IV criteria.
items.reasoning: Confounders were defined using standard clinical criteria.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Information is entered into this database by the neurologist at the time of initial consultation
items.reasoning: Confounders were measured by a specialist during clinical care, ensuring high reliability.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All children were evaluated by the same physician (M.I.S.) in a similar fashion.
items.reasoning: The setting and assessor were consistent for all subjects.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Missing data handling for confounders is not discussed.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study did not use design-stage methods like matching or stratification; it relied on statistical adjustment.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Factors predictive of remission were modeled using Cox regression analysis. ... Logistic regression analyses were used to assess factors predictive of a poor outcome or intractability at outcome. In this case, the duration of follow-up was incorporated into the model as a covariate
items.reasoning: Multivariable modeling was used to adjust for the identified confounders.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods (Cox and Logistic regression) are appropriate for the longitudinal and categorical outcomes. The authors report effect sizes (HR/OR) with 95% CIs and provide Kaplan-Meier curves. There is no evidence of selective reporting, as both 3-month and 12-month predictive models are presented.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Statistical analysis was performed using Statistical Package for Social Sciences software... Factors predictive of remission were modeled using Cox regression analysis. ... Logistic regression analyses were used to assess factors predictive of a poor outcome
items.reasoning: The analytical plan is clearly described.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: The variables entered into the Cox regression and logistic regression models were [LIST]... Two separate analyses were performed to identify factors 3 and 12 months after initiating medication
items.reasoning: The variables selected are clinically relevant and the strategy of looking at different time points (3 vs 12 months) is methodologically sound for early prediction.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Cox regression analysis was used to compensate for the bias toward remission associated with a longer duration of followup
items.reasoning: Cox regression is the gold standard for time-to-event data in prognosis studies.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: For Cox regression analyses, the hazard ratio is quoted followed by the 95% confidence interval.
items.reasoning: The authors report results for all outcomes (remission, poor outcome, intractability) and provide both significant and non-significant findings (e.g., seizure frequency before treatment).

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
